How to Fix a Hacked WordPress Website: 8 Steps from A to Z

A hacked website rarely looks hacked at first. Most infections we clean start with a small symptom: a strange redirect on mobile, a Google warning, an email from the host, a spike in spam signups, or pages ranking for pharmacy keywords you never wrote. Behind that symptom is usually the same pattern: an outdated plugin, theme, or weak login that let an attacker upload a PHP backdoor, inject code into wp-config.php, .htaccess, theme files, or the database, and then quietly use your site for spam, phishing, or SEO hijacking.

Deleting the visible bad file is not a fix. If a single backdoor survives, the site is reinfected within days, often hours. Below is the exact process our malware removal team follows on every WordPress cleanup, in order, so nothing is missed. Work through the steps one at a time, or use the View all steps link to read the full guide.

Step 1 of 8

Confirm the hack and take stock of the damage

Before touching a single file, find out how the site is compromised. Guessing leads to half-cleanups. In 10 minutes you can usually see the shape of the attack.

  • Open Google Search Console and check Security Issues, plus the URL inspection tool for pages you did not create.
  • Load the site from a mobile device and from an incognito window. Redirect malware often hides from logged-in admins.
  • Search Google for site:yourdomain.com and look for pharmacy, casino, or foreign-language pages.
  • Run a remote scan (Sucuri SiteCheck, VirusTotal) and note every flagged URL and blacklist.
  • Read your host's warning email carefully. It usually names the exact infected files.

Write down every symptom. This list is how you will verify the cleanup actually worked in Step 7.

Step 2 of 8

Put the site in maintenance mode and back up everything, even the infected copy

It sounds backwards to back up a hacked site, but you need it. The infected copy is your evidence, your rollback, and your only source for content added since the last clean backup.

  • Enable maintenance mode or a temporary holding page so visitors stop being served malware and Google stops crawling it.
  • Download the full wp-content folder, wp-config.php, .htaccess, and a database export via phpMyAdmin or your host's panel.
  • Locate your oldest clean backup (UpdraftPlus, host snapshots). Check its date against when the symptoms started.
  • Do not restore yet. Most reinfections happen because the backup was already compromised or the entry point was never fixed.

Step 3 of 8

Lock the doors: reset every password, key, and session

Attackers rarely rely on one way in. While you are cleaning, they may still be logged in. Cut off every access path at once.

  • Change passwords for WordPress admin, hosting/cPanel, FTP/SFTP, the database user, and your domain registrar.
  • Go to Users and remove any administrator you do not recognize. Check for accounts with odd emails or role changes.
  • Regenerate the security keys and salts in wp-config.php. This logs out every session, including the attacker's.
  • Revoke unused application passwords, API keys, and third-party connections.
  • Check .htaccess and hosting settings for unauthorized cron jobs and redirect rules.

Step 4 of 8

Find the malware: scan files and the database

This is where most DIY cleanups fail. Malware scanners catch known signatures; they miss obfuscated backdoors and database injections. Combine automated scanning with manual checks.

  • Compare WordPress core against official checksums (wp core verify-checksums via WP-CLI or a plugin like Wordfence).
  • List files modified in the last 30 days. Injected code is usually recent and sits in wp-includes, wp-content/uploads, theme functions.php, or index.php.
  • Look for PHP files inside the uploads folder. There should be none.
  • Search files for eval(, base64_decode(, gzinflate(, str_rot13(, and long single-line strings.
  • Scan the database: wp_options (siteurl, home, active_plugins, widget entries), wp_posts for injected scripts and iframes, and wp_users for hidden admins.

Keep a list of every infected file and table row. You will clean them next and re-verify after.

Step 5 of 8

Clean the infection and remove every backdoor

The rule is replace, do not repair. Editing infected files by hand leaves fragments behind. Fresh copies from the source are always cleaner.

  • Delete wp-admin and wp-includes entirely and upload fresh copies from WordPress.org for the same version.
  • Delete every plugin and theme folder and reinstall them from the official repository or the vendor. Remove anything nulled, abandoned, or unused.
  • Rebuild .htaccess from a clean default and inspect wp-config.php line by line.
  • Remove PHP files from uploads, and strip injected scripts from posts, options, and widgets with a careful search and replace on the database.
  • Delete unknown cron jobs, hidden files (names starting with a dot), and folders outside the WordPress structure.

Then run Step 4 again. A clean rescan is the only proof the backdoors are gone.

Step 6 of 8

Close the hole that let the hacker in

Cleaning without fixing the entry point is a temporary fix. Check the timeline you built in Step 1 against your access and error logs to find the cause.

  • Update WordPress core, every plugin, every theme, and PHP to a supported version. Most hacks exploit a vulnerability that was already patched.
  • Check the WPScan database for your plugin list. Replace any plugin with an unpatched known vulnerability.
  • Fix file permissions: 644 for files, 755 for folders, 440 or 600 for wp-config.php.
  • Disable file editing in the dashboard with DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT.
  • If you share hosting with other sites, scan them too. Cross-site contamination on one account is common.

Step 7 of 8

Restore, harden, and get off the blacklists

With the site clean and patched, bring it back online, then prove to Google and your host that it is safe.

  • Take the site out of maintenance mode and walk through your symptom list from Step 1 on desktop and mobile.
  • In Google Search Console, submit a Request Review under Security Issues. Reviews typically clear in 1 to 3 days when the site is truly clean.
  • Reply to your host's abuse ticket with the cleanup summary so the suspension is lifted.
  • Add a web application firewall (Cloudflare or a security plugin), enable two-factor authentication, limit login attempts, and rename or protect the login URL.
  • Set up daily off-site backups and file-change monitoring so the next attempt is caught in hours, not months.

Step 8 of 8

Do you still need help? We can fix it today

If any of these steps feel risky, or you have already cleaned the site once and it came back, stop. Every hour a hacked site stays live costs you rankings, customer trust, and sometimes your hosting account. Hacked Website? Here’s What to Do Next

A hacked website can quickly turn into a business problem. You may see spam redirects, strange pages in Google, browser security warnings, unauthorized users, missing files, or a sudden drop in traffic. In some cases, your hosting company may even suspend the site.

WevTEC Fix Website Issues helps businesses across the USA clean, restore, and secure hacked websites. We work with WordPress, WooCommerce, ecommerce stores, PHP websites, custom-built sites, and other platforms. Our goal is simple: find what happened, remove the threat, get the website working properly again, and close the security gaps that allowed the problem to happen.

 

How Do You Fix a Hacked Website?

Find out how the site was compromised, remove every infected file and backdoor, close the security hole, then get the site off any blacklists. The step-by-step guide at the top of this page walks through all eight steps for WordPress.

If a site keeps getting reinfected after a cleanup, a hidden backdoor or an unpatched vulnerability was almost certainly missed. That is the most common reason we are called in after someone else has tried.

Why Is My Website Redirecting to Spam Websites?

Unexpected redirects are a common sign of a compromised website. A visitor may click your normal website address and suddenly be sent to a gambling site, pharmacy page, phishing page, fake store, or another unrelated domain.

This can happen because of:

  • Malicious JavaScript

  • Infected plugins or themes

  • Modified PHP files

  • Database injections

  • Compromised administrator accounts

  • Hidden server-level malware

Removing the redirect is only part of the job. The source of the infection also needs to be found so the redirect does not return.

Why Is Google Showing Strange Pages From My Website?

Hackers sometimes create pages that the website owner never sees inside the normal website dashboard. These pages may contain gambling terms, pharmaceutical products, foreign-language keywords, fake products, or other spam.

Google can discover and index these URLs, which may result in hundreds or thousands of unwanted pages appearing under your domain.

The cleanup process may involve removing the malicious content, deleting injected code, fixing redirects, cleaning the database, reviewing indexing problems, and checking Google Search Console for security or spam-related issues.

Can a Website Hack Hurt Google Rankings?

Yes. A hacked website can affect search visibility in several ways.

Malware may create spam pages, redirect visitors, slow down the website, cause downtime, trigger browser warnings, or interfere with Google’s ability to crawl legitimate pages. Search engines may also remove or reduce visibility for pages they believe are unsafe.

After the malware is removed, the SEO damage should be reviewed separately. Hacked URLs, bad redirects, indexing problems, and security warnings can sometimes continue even after the website itself appears normal.

How Do You Recover SEO After a Website Hack?

SEO recovery starts with a completely clean website. Once the infection is removed, we look for issues that may still be affecting search visibility.

This can include:

  • Hacked or spam URLs indexed by Google

  • Malicious redirects

  • Deleted or altered pages

  • Google Search Console security warnings

  • Incorrect canonical tags

  • Damaged internal links

  • Indexing problems

  • Search traffic drops after the attack

The goal is to return the site to a clean, stable condition and help search engines recognize the legitimate website again.

Can a Hacked Website Be Restored?

In many cases, yes.

A hacked website does not automatically need to be rebuilt. Depending on the condition of the site, it may be possible to clean the existing installation, repair damaged files, restore specific components, or use a verified clean backup.

A backup should not be restored blindly. If the backup was created after the website was already infected, restoring it can bring the malware back.

Should I Restore a Backup or Clean the Website?

That depends on when the backup was created and how the website was compromised.

A clean backup can be useful, especially if the current website has extensive damage. However, the original security weakness still needs to be fixed. Otherwise, the restored website may be hacked again.

In many situations, the best approach is to inspect the current site first, identify the infection source, and then decide whether cleanup or restoration is safer.

Can You Remove Hidden Backdoors?

Yes. Hidden backdoors are one of the main reasons hacked websites become infected again after a basic cleanup.

Backdoors can be placed inside:

  • WordPress core files

  • Plugins and themes

  • Upload folders

  • PHP files

  • Database entries

  • Configuration files

  • Server directories

We look for unauthorized code and access points that may allow an attacker to return after the visible malware is removed.

Can My Ecommerce Website Be Repaired After Malware?

Most ecommerce websites can be repaired after a malware infection, depending on the amount of damage.

We can investigate problems such as:

  • Checkout pages behaving incorrectly

  • Malicious scripts

  • Spam redirects

  • Compromised administrator accounts

  • Infected product or database content

  • Suspicious files

  • Website or hosting suspensions

Because ecommerce websites may handle customer information and payment-related functions, the site should be carefully tested after cleanup.

How Long Does Hacked Website Repair Take?

Many common website infections can be diagnosed and repaired the same day. The exact time depends on the size of the website, the type of malware, the hosting environment, and how deeply the infection has spread.

A small WordPress infection may be resolved relatively quickly. A large ecommerce site, multiple infected websites under one hosting account, or server-level malware may require more work.

How Much Does Hacked Website Repair Cost?

The cost depends on the website and the type of infection.

Factors can include:

  • Website platform

  • Number of infected files

  • Database involvement

  • Server access

  • Multiple infected websites

  • Hosting suspension

  • SEO spam damage

  • Whether previous cleanup attempts were unsuccessful

At WevTEC Fix Website Issues, we first review the problem so you know what needs to be repaired before moving forward.

Simpler infections usually fall in our single-fix range of to 0. Severe infections with database damage usually cost 0 to 0. You pay after the site is restored.

Can Someone Clean My WordPress Website Today?

In many cases, yes.

If the necessary website and hosting access is available, our team can begin diagnosing the problem quickly. Many WordPress malware infections can be cleaned and restored the same day, although heavily compromised sites may require additional work.

Is Remote Hacked Website Repair Safe?

Website repair is commonly performed remotely because the files, database, hosting account, and server are already online.

We use the access needed to diagnose and repair the issue, and credentials should be updated after the work is completed. For sensitive websites, access should always be limited to what is necessary for the repair.

How Do I Stop My Website From Getting Hacked Again?

There is no single setting that prevents every future attack, but good security practices can greatly reduce risk.

After cleanup, we may recommend:

  • Updating WordPress, plugins, themes, or other software

  • Removing unused plugins or extensions

  • Changing administrator and hosting passwords

  • Reviewing user accounts

  • Correcting file permissions

  • Securing vulnerable forms or scripts

  • Maintaining regular backups

  • Adding appropriate firewall or security protection

  • Monitoring the website for suspicious changes

The important part is fixing the original vulnerability, not just removing the visible malware.

Who Can Fix My Hacked Website?

WevTEC Fix Website Issues provides hacked website repair, malware removal, WordPress cleanup, ecommerce repair, security recovery, and SEO cleanup for businesses nationwide.

We are Houston-based and have been helping businesses with website repair since 2013. We work remotely with clients across the USA and support WordPress, WooCommerce, PHP, ecommerce, and custom website platforms.

Website Hacked? Get It Checked Before the Damage Spreads

If your website is redirecting visitors, showing security warnings, displaying strange Google results, losing traffic, or has been suspended by your hosting company, early diagnosis can help limit further damage.
